sourcedFrom: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 (2003)
cleanIntro: The Great Plains Hunter comes apart at the hooked breech: drop the wedges, cock the hammer, and the barrel lifts out of the stock muzzle-first with the breech hook sliding free of the tang. Nothing is unscrewed — Lyman cleans the breech plug in place and publishes no procedure for removing it. This rifle's barrel is held by TWO wedges.

steps.title: Deprime before you handle the rifle
steps.action: Take the cap off the nipple before checking or working on the rifle. A muzzleloader with a ball down the bore and no cap is still charged, but a capped one is a gun that can fire.
steps.prose: Lyman gives this as field advice for checking a seated projectile, and it is the same discipline that applies before a cleaning session — the cap comes off first, then you investigate.
steps.quote: Hunters, in particular, should check the position of the projectile in the barrel at regular intervals when in the field. Decap/deprime before checking, though.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Some Words of Caution, item 5, printed p.3

steps.title: Do not trust half-cock as a safety
steps.action: If you are resting the hammer at half-cock while you work, test it: pull the trigger and confirm the hammer does not fall. Lyman states outright that half-cock is not a safety.
steps.prose: This rifle has no manual safety at all — the half-cock notch is the only thing resembling one, and the manual declines to call it that.
steps.quote: Before relying on the half-cock position, make sure the hammer will not fall when the trigger is pulled. Note: half-cock is not a “safety!”
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Some Words of Caution, item 10, printed p.3
steps.warn: Half-cock is a mechanical notch that can fail or be worn. It is not a substitute for an empty, uncapped rifle.

steps.title: Know which barrel you have
steps.action: The Hunter is the fast-twist Great Plains: a 1 in 32" barrel meant for conicals and sabots rather than the patched round ball the 1 in 60" standard Great Plains barrel is cut for.
steps.prose: Twist rate decides what the rifle shoots well, and it is the only thing separating this model from the standard Great Plains Rifle. Everything below about taking it apart and cleaning it is common to both.
steps.quote: The Great Plains Hunter features a 1 in 32" fast twist barrel for conicals or sabots.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Lyman Great Plains Rifle and Great Plains Hunter, printed p.22

steps.title: The Great Plains section is this rifle’s section
steps.action: Lyman prints the Hunter under a joint heading with the Great Plains Rifle and states plainly that it carries the same feature set. That is what licenses using the Great Plains procedures on it.
steps.prose: This matters because the book holds several unrelated guns. The Hunter is not merely printed near the Great Plains Rifle — the manufacturer says it is a version of it.
steps.quote: The Great Plains Hunter has all of the high quality features of our classic Great Plains Rifle.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Lyman Catalog Section, printed p.40

steps.title: Drive out BOTH barrel wedges
steps.action: The Great Plains Hunter is a Great Plains rifle, and a Great Plains barrel is retained by TWO wedges through the forearm, not one. Drive both out before you try to lift the barrel.
steps.prose: This is the difference that matters between the rifles in this book: the Trade Rifle and the Deerstalker take one wedge, the Great Plains guns take two. Lifting against a wedge you forgot is how a forearm splits.
steps.caution: Leave one wedge in place and the barrel will not come free — do not lever it.
steps.quote: Wedges (One for Trade & Deerstalker two for Great Plains)
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Special Product Information, Check List for Lyman Black Powder Guns, printed p.2

steps.title: Lift the barrel out of the stock, muzzle first
steps.action: Pull the ramrod, drive out the wedge, draw the hammer to full cock, then lift the barrel muzzle-first out of the stock. The hooked breech slips straight out of the tang — nothing else has to come apart.
steps.prose: Full cock is what clears the nipple and hammer so the breech can rise out of the tang unit. The hook is a slip fit by design; if it resists, the hammer is not far enough back or a wedge is still in.
steps.quote: The Lyman Great Plains Rifle, Trade Rifle, Deerstalker or Plains Pistol may be easily disassembled for cleaning by removing the ramrod, driving out the barrel wedge in the forearm, drawing the hammer to full cock and lifting the barrel (muzzle first) out of stock. The hooked breech will slip right out of the tang unit with no further disassembly needed.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Disassembly and Cleaning of Rifles and Plains Pistol, printed p.13

steps.title: Or clean it without taking it apart
steps.action: Taking the barrel out is optional. You can clean the rifle fully assembled, provided you keep water and solvent out of the stock and the lock.
steps.prose: Assembled cleaning is the trade: no wedge to drive, but you are working next to a wood stock and an exposed lock with hot water. Most people who shoot the rifle often take the barrel out precisely to avoid that risk.
steps.quote: Of course, these Lyman guns can be cleaned without any disassembly but care should be taken to prevent water and solvents from entering the stock or lock mechanism.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Disassembly and Cleaning of Rifles and Plains Pistol, printed p.13

steps.title: Clean after every session, without exception
steps.action: Clean the rifle after each shooting session. Black powder fouling is corrosive and will pit the bore if left.
steps.prose: This is not a round-count schedule. One session, however few shots, earns a full clean.
steps.quote: You must clean your rifle or pistol after each shooting session to prevent rust and corrosion from damaging the metal parts.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Disassembly and Cleaning of Rifles and Plains Pistol, printed p.13

steps.title: Hot soapy water — the traditional method
steps.action: Scrub the bore with a strong solution of hot soapy water and wipe the powder fouling off the other metal parts. Then flush the barrel with the hottest clean water you have and dry everything.
steps.prose: The heat is doing a job beyond rinsing the soap out: it warms the steel so the barrel dries itself from the inside as the water runs off. A barrel flushed cold stays damp in the breech.
steps.quote: HOT SOAPY WATER–The traditional way to clean a muzzleloader. 1. Scrub the bore with a strong solution of hot soapy water. Wipe all powder fouling from other metal parts. 2. Flush the barrel with the hottest clean water available. This not only removes the soap but also heats the steel which helps in the drying process. 3. Dry all parts.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Two Cleaning Techniques, printed p.13

steps.title: Or modern black powder solvents
steps.action: Scrub the bore with a brass brush and plenty of patches and wipe down all metal parts. Then wipe the bore dry with clean patches on the supplied jag, dry all metal parts, and oil.
steps.prose: The cleaning jag that came with the rifle screws onto the end of the ramrod and is already sized to the bore — it holds a patch tightly enough that it will not shed one down the barrel.
steps.quote: 1. Scrub the bore with brass brush and lots of patches. Wipe down all metal parts. 2. Using plenty of clean patches, wipe the bore dry. All guns are supplied with a cleaning jag of the proper size. The jag screws into the end of the ramrod and will securely hold cleaning patches. Dry all metal parts. 3. Apply oil to all metal parts and reassemble.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Two Cleaning Techniques, Modern Solvents, printed p.13

steps.title: Reach the powder channel with a .35 cal brush
steps.action: The breech plug's powder channel is narrower than the bore, so your cleaning jag will not enter it. Use a .35 calibre brush or a slotted-tip rod to get into that pocket.
steps.prose: This is the one spot that a normal bore routine misses entirely, and it is where fouling sits closest to the ignition path. Note what Lyman does NOT say here: the plug is cleaned in place. There is no instruction anywhere in this book to unscrew it.
steps.quote: Note: The powder channel inside the breech plug is smaller than the bore diameter and does not allow the cleaning jag to enter. Lyman recommends the use of a .35 cal. cleaning brush and/or a slotted tip cleaning rod to reach into this area.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Cleaning Note, printed p.13

steps.title: Oil everything and reassemble
steps.action: Put a good coat of oil or a moisture-displacing lubricant on all metal parts and reassemble. A silicone gun rag is the manual’s recommendation for the outside.
steps.prose: Then check it again over the next few days. Black powder residue that survived the clean announces itself as fresh rust within about seventy-two hours, and catching it then is far cheaper than catching it next season.
steps.quote: Apply a good coat of oil or moisture-displacing lubricant to all metal parts and reassemble. A silicone gun rag is excellent for treating the exterior of the muzzleloader.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Two Cleaning Techniques, Hot Soapy Water step 4, printed p.13

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: Barrel out, bore scrubbed and dried, powder channel reached with the .35 brush, everything oiled and back together. That is the routine clean for the Great Plains Hunter.
steps.prose: Inspect it again over the next few days before calling the job finished.
steps.quote: Inspect for the next few days just to be safe.
steps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Two Cleaning Techniques, printed p.13

deepSteps.title: Use the snail's clean out screw
deepSteps.action: The Great Plains pattern carries a Hawken-style percussion snail with a clean out screw. Backing it out opens the fouled corner of the ignition path that no rod reaches from the muzzle.
deepSteps.prose: Lyman lists this among the Great Plains features, and separately states that the Hunter has all of them — which is what carries the clean out screw across to this rifle. The Trade Rifle and Deerstalker descriptions in this book list no such screw.
deepSteps.quote: Each Great Plains Rifle offers such high quality features as a 32", 1 in 60" twist barrel for patched ball and hunting loads, double set triggers, Hawken style percussion “snail” with clean out screw and reliable coil spring lock with correct lock plate.
deepSteps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Lyman Great Plains Rifle and Great Plains Hunter, printed p.22

deepSteps.title: Confirm the lock section covers your rifle
deepSteps.action: Check the heading before you use anything in the lock section: it is written for the Lyman Great Plains, Trade and Deerstalker percussion models.
deepSteps.prose: This book carries several different guns and a pistol, and the sections are not interchangeable. Reading the heading is the check.
deepSteps.quote: Percussion Lock Assembly (For Lyman Great Plains, Trade and Deerstalker Percussion Models)
deepSteps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Lock Assemblies, printed p.30

deepSteps.title: Cock the hammer BEFORE removing the lock
deepSteps.action: If you are taking the lock assembly out of the stock, pull the hammer to full cock first. Lyman is explicit that skipping this damages the wood.
deepSteps.prose: At rest the hammer sits down against the nipple and the lock's internals are relaxed into the mortise; drawing it out in that state levers the tumbler against the stock. Full cock lifts everything clear.
deepSteps.caution: Wood damage will result if the hammer is not at full cock. There is no recovering an inletted mortise once it has been torn.
deepSteps.quote: Note: Pull hammer to full cock before removing lock assembly from the stock. Wood damage will result if this is not done.
deepSteps.cite: Lyman User's Guide for Black Powder Products — ©2003 Lyman Products Corporation, (3-03) #6985043 — Lock Assemblies, Percussion Lock Assembly, printed p.30

cleaning.name: Bore
tasks: Hot soapy water, strong solution, scrub the bore
Flush with the hottest clean water available so the steel heats and dries
Or: brass brush and plenty of patches with a black powder solvent
Wipe the bore dry with clean patches on the supplied jag
A .35 cal brush or slotted tip into the breech plug's powder channel — the jag will not enter it

cleaning.name: Lock and exterior
tasks: Wipe all powder fouling off the external metal parts
Keep water and solvent out of the stock and lock mechanism
Oil or moisture-displacing lubricant on all metal parts
Silicone gun rag over the exterior

cleaning.name: Follow-up
tasks: Inspect the rifle again over the next few days for rust that has come back through

reassembly: Slide the hooked breech back into the tang unit with the hammer at full cock and the barrel entering the stock breech-first.
Seat the barrel down into the forearm channel.
Drive BOTH wedges back through the forearm — the Great Plains pattern takes two, not one.
Return the ramrod to its thimbles.
Lower the hammer onto an empty, uncapped nipple.
fncheck: With the rifle uncapped and unloaded, bring the hammer to half-cock and pull the trigger — the hammer must not fall. Then check that the hammer falls cleanly from full cock and that the barrel is seated with both wedges fully home.
